chapter_theme: The great battle of the Earth-lady ilampakam: the clash of horses, chariots and elephants, the arrows that darken the sky, the Earth veiling her eyes in a blanket of blood, the slain bridegrooms feasted on by ghouls and jackals, and the duels in which Vijayan's fight ends Madanan, Buddhisenan seizes kings by the hair, Devadattan routs the Magadha king and Sridattan kills the Kalinga king.

cast.role: the Earth goddess, who in the battle-poetry veils her eyes from the slaughter
Kattiyangaran's ally who urges force; killed in the final war (called மன்மதன் in 2246)
prince of Hemamapuram, Civakan's friend, who fights in his war
the war elephant Manmathan climbs in 2248
Civakan's companion, a Brahmin (நான்மறையாளன்), a fighter in the war (written புத்திமா சேனன் in 2249)
one of Civakan's companions (written தேவமா தத்தன் in 2250)
the king of the Magadhas, fighting on Kattiyangaran's side, who flees
merchant of Rajamapuram, Civakan's friend, a fighter in the war
the king of the Kalingas, fighting on Kattiyangaran's side, killed by Sridattan

2227.reading: The narrator says the severed heads of warriors falling with their precious garlands on the field looked like dark ripe palmyra fruit shaken down when the wind strikes a palm grove.
2227.event: Warriors' heads are struck off and fall on the field.

2228.reading: The narrator describes the war horses, impatient of the stable, golden-garlanded, plumed on the forehead with yak-tail, swift enough to outrun arrows, young and evenly paired, as they go into the fight with their riders.
2228.event: The cavalry rides into the battle.

2229.reading: The narrator describes the chariots, their hubs shaped by the sharp chisel, gold-rimmed and flashing like lightning from a cloud, as they close wheel to wheel with the best of the enemy's chariots.
2229.event: The chariots close with one another.

2230.reading: The narrator describes the war elephants, painted with collyrium and fed on rice balls, their drums beating like Death's, looking like mountains with wings, clashing like cloud-climbed hills.

2231.reading: The royal elephants crash into one another so that fire flies, like great sea ships that have snapped their ropes in a contrary wind and run together with no way out.

2232.reading: The loosed arrows crowd the sky until the sun's rays are hidden and darkness spreads, and in that darkness the gleam of killing spears and the gems on kings' crowns burn like sunlight.
2232.event: Arrows darken the sky over the field.

2233.reading: The narrator says that the Earth goddess, with jewelled breasts, saying she cannot look with her eyes at such cruel things, covered herself with a single red blanket, that is, the blood that now covers the field.
2233.event: The field is covered in blood, which the poet makes the Earth's red veil.
2233.nuance: The conceit turns the reddened ground into a modesty: Earth, the bride the hero is to win in this ilampakam of the Earth-lady (மண்மகள்), veils her eyes from the war fought for her. Her words are reported speech inside the narration (எனா).

2234.reading: Men whose broad garlanded chests had been ploughed by the jewelled breasts of women with earrings are now ploughed by the killing tusks of rutting elephants, and bathe in blood.
2234.event: Warriors are gored by elephants and lie in blood.
2234.nuance: The verb உழப்பட்ட is used twice, once for love and once for the tusk, so the same chest is worked over first by pleasure and then by death.

2235.reading: Warriors whose dark hair had worn the wedding garlands their brides strung with soft fingers, now washed by blood, wear garlands of entrails and make a great feast for the corpse-garlanded ghoul-woman.
2235.event: Slain warriors lie in blood, a feast for the ghouls.
2235.nuance: The verse runs four garlands in a row (மணமாலை, இணர்மாலை, நிணமாலை, பிணமாலை): the bride's garland gives way to the entrail-garland, so the wedding becomes the ghoul's banquet.

2236.reading: The ankleted feet of kings who never lost a battle, cut off with their anklets by flashing swords as they raised their bangled arms and spat fire at one another, writhe in the blood like sharks in the dark sea.
2236.event: Kings' feet are cut off in the sword fight.

2237.reading: Elephants whose armour has been pierced and who are swarmed with arrows, maddened, crush the bannered chariots and rise carrying the rolling wheels on them, spreading like hills the sun has reached.

2238.reading: The cut trunks of rutting elephants lying under tall garlanded parasols in thick blood look like the white moon of the high sky pulled down to earth together with a dark serpent.
2238.event: Elephants' trunks are cut off and lie under the fallen parasols.
2238.nuance: The white parasol is the moon and the dark trunk the eclipse serpent; the image of a fallen light swallowed by a serpent returns in 2245 and 2251 for the fallen captains.

2239.reading: The elephants, their black colour lost under a cloak of blood, look like vermilion mountains, and the blood that bubbles out where they charge looks like vermilion falls on every side.

2240.reading: Men lie with an elephant for a pillow at the head and a maned horse at the feet, having paid off the debt of the red rice, still gripping their angry swords on the cloth they wore, their waist cords glinting, while jackals come up in fear and howl over them.
2240.event: The dead lie on the field and jackals gather and howl.

claims.claim: a warrior who dies in battle has paid the debt he owes for the rice his lord fed him

2240.nuance: செஞ்சோற்றுக் கடன் names the fighter's death as repayment of a debt, not as glory; the only mourners in the verse are jackals.

2241.reading: Warriors bite down their lips, the coral mouths that gave nectar to their lovers, as if saying they will not give them to alien birds to eat, and lie with gold ear-studs and earrings gleaming, broad-chested, like sleeping Vidyadharas.
2241.event: The fallen warriors lie with lips bitten.
2241.nuance: The bitten lip is the warrior's fury at death; the poet reads it as a lover's refusal to let the mouth his beloved kissed be eaten by birds.

2242.reading: Small jackals dragging entrails through the mire of fat and flesh look like fierce dogs pulling at chains, and birds rising with bangled arms look like Garuda rising with hooded snakes.
2242.event: Jackals and birds feed on the slain.

2243.reading: Like lions rolling on the ground when thunder strikes the hill, the royal elephants, with flawless gold face-plates, fight in a rising cloud of dust, are destroyed and sink with their kings into the killing field.
2243.event: Royal elephants fall with their kings on the field.
2243.nuance: Line 2's நிரையுளை அரிநன்மா may be maned lions (the simile) or fine maned horses; read as the simile, it keeps the verse's subject the royal elephants of line 4.

2244.reading: The chest that women with kuvalai eyes and long hair had embraced, sandal-smeared, chains tangling, is now embraced by the sword, and the jewel lying in the flowing blood looks like a young crescent in a wide red sky.
2244.event: A warrior lies slain in his own blood.
2244.nuance: புல்லிய and புல்ல repeat the verb of embrace: the sword takes the women's place on the same chest.

2245.reading: Like the moon that splits black darkness, swallowed by Rahu and plunging into the sea's waves, Madanan, after churning the long battle and leaping onto an elephant's forehead, falls at the mouth of a fierce sword, and Vijayan wins the victory of the fight.
2245.event: Madanan falls by the sword and Vijayan wins the fight.
2245.nuance: The syntax leaves open whether Madanan or Vijayan leaps onto the elephant's forehead; the next three verses tell the fight at length and end it on the elephant's tusk, not a sword, so 2245 reads as the summary and 2246 to 2248 as its telling.

2246.reading: The youth called Manmathan, on his chariot drawn by bell-ringing horses, rains arrows and roars like Death; when the death-dealing hero cuts the bow on his golden chariot, he leaps down like an angry lion from a golden hill and stands on the ground.
2246.event: Manmathan fights from his chariot; when his bow is cut he leaps down to fight on foot.
2246.nuance: மன்மதன் is taken as the same man as 2245's மதனன் (both are names of Kama), and the bow-cutter as Vijayan; the verse names neither identification.

2247.reading: Three arrows sink spitting fire into his forehead and he wears them on his brow like a garland, like gems set on coral; pressing his teeth into his red lip, he draws his sword.
2247.event: Struck in the forehead by three arrows, Manmathan bites his lip and draws his sword.

2248.reading: Lifting his blade on his shoulder he climbs onto the elephant; it strikes him with its long trunk so that he falls face down on the ground, gores him and lifts him torn in two, and the gold-chested warrior, twisting, swings his sword and dies upon the tusk.
2248.event: Manmathan climbs the elephant, is thrown and gored, strikes with his sword and dies on its tusk.
2248.nuance: Whose elephant it is, and whether the one who dies on the tusk is Manmathan or the elephant's rider, the verse does not say; this reading follows the run of 2246 to 2247.

2249.reading: Buddhisenan, the man of the four Vedas, with honey-dripping garland, like a heap of wrought gold ornaments, surges up and from his chariot with wheels like a potter's seizes kings by their tufts, like the forehead-eyed god who loosed the blazing fire-arrow.
2249.event: Buddhisenan drives his chariot through the kings and seizes them by the hair.
2249.nuance: The companion is called நான்மறையாளன், a Brahmin, and the Jain epic likens his fury to Siva burning the three cities with a fiery arrow, using the Saiva myth purely as a simile of rage.

2250.reading: Devamathattan, like a hill of campaka flowers, fiercely sending lives into the sky, charges like a lion that strikes a rutting elephant so that the earth splits, and the Magadha king, seeing his sea-like army flee, in shame sheathes his spear.
2250.event: Devadattan routs the Magadha army, and its king, ashamed, sheathes his spear.
2250.nuance: The Magadha king's shame ends in sheathing the spear, not in death: the verse lets the defeated king withdraw.

2251.reading: Sridattan, with small flowers in his hair, strikes his angry golden sword into the forehead of the Kalinga king among the kings, and the king falls, his earrings, ornaments and necklace blazing, like the bright sun falling into the sea together with a planet.
2251.event: Sridattan kills the Kalinga king with his sword.

links.note: In 257 Madanan told the council he settles things only by the sword, never by the mouth; in 2245 he falls at the mouth of a sword (வாளின்வாய்) in the war that the usurpation he urged has brought on.
links.teaches: The man who refused talk for the sword dies by the sword's 'mouth', so the epic answers his boast with its own wording and makes his death the fruit of his counsel.

links.note: Madanan falls like the moon swallowed by Rahu plunging into the sea; the Kalinga king falls like the sun dropping into the sea with a planet.
links.teaches: The two eclipse similes make the enemy's captains the moon and the sun of their side, so their two deaths together read as the setting of both lights of Kattiyangaran's host.

links.note: In 803, at his first battle, Civakan watches a ghoul dress herself in the slain and laughs with delight; in 2235 the same ghoul's feast is made from bridegrooms whose wedding garlands their brides had strung.
links.teaches: Where the first battle offers the ghoul's feast as spectacle for the hero's laughter, the final war sets it against the brides' garlands, so the same image now carries the cost of war to the women left behind.

links.note: Kural 780 calls a death that fills the eyes of one's patron with tears worth begging for; 2240's warriors have paid their debt of the red rice, and the only ones who cry over them are jackals.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's logic of a death owed to the lord but removes the weeping patron who gave that death its worth, leaving the debt paid with no one to mourn it.

gains.a: the Kural gives the epic's 'debt of red rice' its moral frame, a death owed in return for being sustained
gains.b: the couplet's patron's tears are shown to be absent on the actual field, where the howling of jackals takes their place

links.note: Puram 26 praises a Pandya who cooked a battlefield sacrifice with crowned heads for the hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in 2235 the slain warriors themselves are the ghoul-woman's feast, their wedding garlands replaced by entrails.
links.teaches: The Sangam battlefield-feast is the victor's rite and his glory, while the Cintamani tells it from the side of the slain, as bridegrooms whose wedding garlands become entrails.

gains.a: the epic's ghoul-feast is placed in the old genre of the battlefield sacrifice it inherits
gains.b: the Puram's feast, sung only from the victor's side, is shown from the dead men's side, where it costs a marriage

links.note: In Puram 19 Death itself runs away ashamed from the field where mothers of old houses weep over their sons; in 2233 the Earth goddess, unable to look at the cruelty, veils herself in a red blanket of blood.
links.teaches: Both poems make a cosmic power recoil from the field, but the Sangam poem turns the recoil into praise of the king's valour, while the epic gives it to the Earth the hero fights to win, so the prize cannot bear the war waged for her.

gains.a: the conceit gains an older pattern in which a cosmic witness flinching from the slaughter measures its scale
gains.b: the Puram's recoil, used there to praise the victor, is shown able to judge the war instead, when the one who flinches is the land being won

links.note: Naladiyar 48 asks those who praise sandal and garlands whether they have not seen vultures tear the body once it breaks; 2244 sets the sandal-smeared chest that women embraced in the blood, embraced now by the sword.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ruined body to turn a man from desire, but the epic shows the same ruin of the beloved body in battle and draws no lesson from it, keeping beauty and slaughter in one image without preaching.

gains.a: the epic's image gains a name for what it shows, the body's adornment undone, which it leaves unspoken
gains.b: the quatrain's argument meets a case where the body is broken by war rather than age, and the poet still sees it as beautiful

source_issues: Verses 2235, 2236, 2238 and 2242 to 2251 were printed in eight half-lines and have been joined into four.
Verse 2230 line 2 prints கொம்மை கொட்வே, apparently for கொட்டவே.
Verse 2246 calls the warrior மன்மதன் where 2245 has மதனன்; they are read as one man.
